items.x_text:
AI chatbots and the US midterms: a Forum AI study of 8 models found almost 40% of election answers had at least one factual error. Gemini gave a Pennsylvania mail-ballot deadline a week too late (via AFP). Check your official election office.

#AI #Misinformation
items.ig_caption:
~40% of AI election answers had an error. 🗳️

What AFP reported (2 Nov), a day before the US midterms:
→ Forum AI tested 8 AI models: almost 40% of answers to election questions had at least one factual error
→ Voting logistics (deadlines, how to vote) went wrong more often than questions about candidates
→ Gemini 3.6 Flash gave 3 November as Pennsylvania's deadline to request a mail-in ballot. The real deadline was a week earlier
→ Claude credited Rep. Don Davis as a "former school superintendent", mixing him up with someone else
→ 2 in 5 Americans have used AI tools for election information (National Conference on Citizenship)
→ The upside: a Brennan Center study found leading chatbots rejected common voting-machine conspiracy theories

The takeaway: use AI to explain, not to decide where, when or how. Dates, deadlines and polling places come from your official election office.

cover.hook: Frontier Airlines says scammers are emailing its customers right now.
cover.sub: Its notice: "We are aware of an active email phishing campaign targeting our customers." No breach confirmed.

slides.title: What Frontier says
slides.body: Frontier does not email customers asking for flight, reservation, payment or contact details. Its advice: don't click the links, don't enter payment or login details, don't reply.

slides.title: Why people noticed
slides.body: Passengers posting on Reddit say the scam emails quoted real names, itineraries and confirmation numbers (per RuntimeWire, 1 Nov). The thread trended on Hacker News. Frontier has not confirmed a data breach.

slides.label: emails from Frontier asking for your flight, payment or contact details

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: A real booking reference makes a fake email feel safe. Scammers who know your trip are more convincing. Treat any 'fix your reservation' email as a lure, however much it knows about you.

slides.title: Do this today
items: Open the airline app or type its URL yourself
Never pay or log in from an emailed link
Shared card details? Call your card issuer
Report suspect travel emails to your security team

#Android #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
One SMS. Zero clicks. Phone service down. 📵

What the researcher disclosed (29 Oct):
→ A malformed WAP Push SMS crashes Android's telephony process (com.android.phone). No tap needed
→ Active calls drop, including emergency calls
→ Carrier redelivery repeated the crash: outages for up to a week in testing; about 20 messages can make a phone unusable
→ Listed as affecting Android 12–17, tested on a Pixel 9 and Samsung Galaxy phones
→ Reported to Google on 5 May 2026; fixed in the October 2026 security update for Android 14–17. Android 12 and 13 get no fix
→ No attacks in the wild reported

What to do: check Settings → Security update and make sure company phones are on the October 2026 patch level or later. Plan to replace devices stuck on Android 12 or 13.

diagram.title: Upload an Image. Get a Webshell.

items.x_text:
How an image upload turns into a webshell: the server saves attacker content as .php in a web folder and runs it. OWASP's fix: allow-list types, rename files, store outside the webroot, re-encode images.

#AppSec #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Upload an image. Get a webshell. 🖼️

How it works, step by step:
→ An attacker sends a file that looks like an image but carries hidden PHP code
→ The site trusts it and saves it as a .php file inside a public folder like /images/
→ The web server runs it. Now the attacker has a webshell: every file, and the database via the config file
→ This is what hit Joomla sites through YOOtheme Pro in October: db8 found at least 3 groups and ~15 webshells on one site
→ The safe path (OWASP): allow-list extensions and check the real file type, rename files with an app-generated name, store uploads outside the webroot or block PHP there, re-encode images
→ Already patched? Updates don't remove backdoors. Look for PHP files in upload folders

Send this to whoever runs your website 👇

Source: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet, db8 (23 Oct 2026)

items.x_text:
YOOtheme Pro CVE-2026-102785 (CVSS 10): a Joomla site was hit 6+ hours before the fix shipped; 3 groups left ~15 webshells, per db8. Update to 5.0.53+, then hunt for PHP files in upload folders. Updating doesn't remove backdoors.

#ZeroDay #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Hacked 6 hours before the patch existed. ⏱️

What we know about CVE-2026-102785 in YOOtheme Pro (CVSS 10):
→ Unauthenticated: attackers write a webshell through the image handler. Affects the Joomla and WordPress builder, fixed in 5.0.53
→ db8 traced one fully updated Joomla site hit at 08:44 on 21 Oct. The fix shipped around 15:00 the same day
→ At least 3 groups fought over that one site: ~15 webshells and backdoors, ~5,600 .htaccess files, a replaced index.php
→ The goal was SEO spam: Google and Bing saw spam pages, visitors saw the normal site
→ Public exploits exist, and as of 2 Nov it was not in CISA's KEV catalog

What to do: update YOOtheme Pro to 5.0.53 or later. Then hunt, because the update doesn't remove backdoors: look for PHP files in images/, media/, cache/ and tmp/, check access logs for FROMFILE= and SAVE=, and run site:yourdomain.com to spot spam pages. Compromised? Restore a clean backup into an empty webroot and rotate passwords and secrets.
